description_full: International Business Machines Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, provides integrated solutions and services in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. It operates through Software, Consulting, Infrastructure, and Financing segments. The Software segment offers hybrid cloud and AI platforms that allow clients to realize their digital and AI transformations across the applications, data, and environments in which they operate. The Consulting segment delivers strategy and technology services and intelligent operations, providing business transformation, technology implementation, managed services, application modernization, and AI-powered solutions. The Infrastructure segment provides on-premises and cloud-based server, and storage solutions, as well as life-cycle services for hybrid cloud infrastructure deployment. The Financing segment offers client and commercial financing, and facilitates IBM clients' acquisition of hardware, software, and services. It operates a data streaming platform. The company has partnerships with various companies, including hyperscalers, service providers, global system integrators, and software and hardware vendors that include Adobe, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Oracle, Salesforce, Samsung Electronics and SAP, and others. It also has a collaboration with Arm Holdings plc to develop new dual-architecture hardware for AI and data intensive workloads; partnership with three.ws to advance ai-powered 3d agent technology; and collaboration with Lightwell to help strengthen open source software supply chain. Additionally, it offers operational resilience, logistics, and future-ready technology to the UK Ministry of Defence through Team ORION. The company was formerly known as Computing-Tabulating-Recording Co. and changed its name to International Business Machines Corporation in 1924. International Business Machines Corporation was incorporated in 1911 and is headquartered in Armonk, New York.

financial_summary: International Business Machines is a mega-cap technology business with a $233.6B market cap on $67.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and -2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 48%.

The business throws off $12.1B in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.25× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.3× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.3×.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Carries more leverage than most Technology peers — a smaller cushion for the inevitable bad year
Significant goodwill (45% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Technology sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 7% over 3 months
Elevated sector volatility (38% annualized) adds uncertainty
Antitrust and platform-regulation risk — the larger the network effect, the larger the regulatory target on its back, and a single consent decree can reset the moat.
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 11% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
64 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible

sect: Its 18% operating margin runs 11pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.78x).
It accounts for 1.5% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 23% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 48% and a beta of 0.78, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.19 vs 5y 0.72), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.1B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 39% in the 2020 crash, 17% in the 2022 bear market and 44% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 4% below its DCF fair value of $257, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $196 to $347 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 21.1 vs 27.4 and P/FCF 19.3 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 31% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $260 on average, 5% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.57).
It runs a 48% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.25x.
ROE of 32% is amplified by 4.7x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 12.3% of revenue on R&D and 2.5% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.3x net debt to EBITDA ($13.6B of cash against $61.3B of debt), with interest covered 6.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.3, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.96 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 45% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.7% over 3 years, -1.7% over 5 years and -1.9% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -4.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.12 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 1.1x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 16%.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 65%.
It returns 2.7% a year to shareholders (2.7% in dividends).
The share count has grown 1.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 64 consecutive years, raising it 1.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 264,300 employees, each generates about $256K of revenue, 0.7x the Technology median, and revenue has fallen 2.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $46K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.4M (29x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
